# Thyroid gland and parathyroid glands

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Basics of endocrinology and metabolism > Thyroid gland and parathyroid glands*

[Original Article Link](/library/i60JkS)

---

## Summary

The <u>thyroid gland</u> is a butterfly-shaped endocrine gland located inferior to the <u>larynx</u> and <u>anterior</u> to the <u>trachea</u>. The <u>thyroid gland</u> develops from the fusion of the <u>median thyroid anlage</u> with the two <u>lateral thyroid anlages</u>, which are derived from the <u>pharyngeal pouches</u>. The <u>thyroid gland</u> is contained by the pretracheal <u>fascia</u> and <u>internal capsule</u>. It receives its arterial supply from the superior and <u>inferior thyroid arteries</u> and drains into the superior, middle, and inferior <u>thyroid</u> <u>veins</u>. The <u>lymphatics</u> drain into the paratracheal and <u>deep cervical lymph nodes</u>. It receives <u>sympathetic</u> innervation via the cervical <u>ganglion</u> and <u>parasympathetic</u> innervation via the <u>vagus nerve</u>. The <u>thyroid gland</u> secretes <u>thyroid hormones</u>, which regulate body metabolism and growth, and <u>calcitonin</u>, which lowers serum <u>calcium</u> and <u>phosphate</u> through inhibition of <u>osteoclasts</u>. <u>Hormone</u> synthesis occurs in the <u>epithelial</u> lining of the <u>thyroid follicles</u>. The <u>epithelial</u> lining consists of follicular (<u>thyroid</u> <u>epithelial</u>) cells, which synthesize <u>thyroid hormone</u>, and parafollicular (C) cells, which synthesize <u>calcitonin</u>.




The <u>parathyroid glands</u> are four, oval-shaped endocrine glands located on the <u>posterior</u> surface of the <u>thyroid gland</u>. They are derived from the third and fourth <u>pharyngeal pouches</u>. The <u>parathyroid glands</u> receive their arterial supply from the <u>inferior thyroid arteries</u> and drain into the <u>thyroid</u> venous plexus. The <u>lymphatics</u> drain into the paratracheal and <u>deep cervical lymph nodes</u>. The <u>parathyroid glands</u> are innervated by the <u>thyroid</u> branch of the cervical <u>ganglia</u>. The <u>parathyroid chief cells</u> secrete <u>parathyroid hormone</u>, which maintains serum <u>calcium</u> and <u>phosphate</u> <u>homeostasis</u> and, furthermore, antagonizes the effect of <u>calcitonin</u> by increasing serum <u>calcium</u> and decreasing serum <u>phosphate</u>. The <u>recurrent laryngeal nerves</u>, <u>parathyroid glands</u>, <u>sympathetic trunks</u>, and the nerves of the <u>carotid sheath</u> are at risk of injury during <u>thyroid surgery</u>.

## Thyroid gland

### Overview




* Characteristics: butterfly-shaped, unpaired endocrine gland composed of two lobes

* Location

* Located anteriorly in the lower part of the neck

* Extends from C5–T1

* Surrounded by pretracheal <u>fascia</u> (along with <u>pharynx</u>, <u>trachea</u>, <u>esophagus</u>)

* Relations of the <u>thyroid gland</u>

* Anteriorly: <u>strap muscles</u> (i.e., sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and omohyoid muscles)

* Medially: the <u>trachea</u>, <u>esophagus</u>, <u>recurrent laryngeal nerve</u> (RLN), and the external branch of the <u>superior laryngeal nerve</u>

* Posteriorly: the <u>parathyroid glands</u>  cricoid <u>cartilage</u>, lower <u>thyroid</u> <u>cartilage</u>, and the <u>carotid sheath</u> with its contents (i.e., <u>internal jugular vein</u>, <u>vagus nerve</u>, and <u>common carotid artery</u>)

* Function

* Production of <u>thyroid hormones</u> essential for regulating metabolism and growth

* <u>Parafollicular cells</u> (<u>C cells</u>) produce <u>calcitonin</u>, which influences <u>calcium homeostasis</u> by lowering serum <u>calcium</u> (<u>PTH</u> <u>antagonism</u>).

> Damage to the <u>recurrent laryngeal nerves</u>, <u>parathyroid glands</u>, <u>sympathetic trunks</u>, and even the nerves of the <u>carotid sheath</u> is possible during <u>thyroidectomy</u> because of the <u>thyroid</u>'s location in the <u>anterior</u> neck.

## Gross anatomy

### Gross anatomy




* The <u>thyroid gland</u> is made up of a left lobe and a right lobe connected by an <u>isthmus</u>.

* An ascending <u>pyramidal lobe</u> is present in ∼ 50% of the population.

* The <u>thyroid gland</u> is encapsulated by:

* Pretracheal <u>fascia</u> (false/surgical capsule)

* <u>Internal capsule</u> (true capsule)

* Inner <u>connective tissue</u> covering that cannot be separated from the gland

* Forms septae, dividing the gland into lobes and lobules

## Function

The <u>thyroid gland</u> produces <u>thyroid hormones</u>, which stimulate metabolism and growth, as well as <u>calcitonin</u>, which decreases bone resorption and is involved in plasma <u>calcium homeostasis</u>.




### <u>Calcitonin</u>




* Function: lowers <u>calcium</u> in serum (see “<u>Hypocalcemia</u>”)

* Bones: inhibits <u>osteoclast</u> activity

* <u>Kidneys</u>: increases excretion of <u>calcium</u> and <u>phosphate</u>

* Intestine: lowers <u>calcium</u> absorption

* The physiological role of <u>calcitonin</u> is low as bone and <u>calcium</u> metabolism are mainly regulated by the <u>parathyroid hormone</u> and <u>vitamin D</u>

* Released in response to increased serum <u>calcium</u> levels

* Clinical significance

* Important as a <u>tumor marker</u> for <u>medullary thyroid cancer</u>

* Acts as a synthetic analog for the <u>treatment of osteoporosis</u> (minimizes bone resorption)

* The precursor <u>procalcitonin</u> plays an increasingly important role as a marker for bacterial infection (e.g., <u>sepsis</u>).





### Thyroid hormones




#### Thyroid hormone synthesis




* The <u>thyroid hormones</u> T<sub>3</sub> (triiodothyronine) and T<sub>4</sub> (thyroxine, <u>tetraiodothyronine</u>) are synthesized by <u>thyrocytes</u> in the <u>thyroid follicles</u>.  [[1]](/library/rp0fIS)
1. * <u>Thyroglobulin</u>, an <u>iodine</u>-free <u>hormone</u> precursor, is stored in the follicular lumen.
2. * Iodide is actively taken up by <u>thyrocytes</u> and transported into the follicular lumen.
3. * Here, <u>thyroid peroxidase</u> catalyzes the iodination of <u>tyrosine</u> residues of <u>thyroglobulin</u>, creating precursors monoiodotyrosine (MIT) and diiodotyrosine (DIT) and eventually the <u>thyroid hormones</u>.
4. * To release T<sub>3</sub> and T<sub>4</sub>, the iodinated <u>thyroglobulin</u> must be taken up again by <u>thyrocytes</u>, where it is broken down by <u>lysosomes</u>, thus releasing attached T<sub>4</sub> and T<sub>3</sub>.
5. * T<sub>4</sub> and T<sub>3</sub> are then transported out of the <u>thyrocyte</u> into the blood.

* More T<sub>4</sub> is produced than T<sub>3</sub> but T<sub>3</sub> is more potent than T<sub>4</sub>.

* Peripheral 5'-deiodinase (or type II iodothyronine deiodinase) in the <u>thyroid</u>, <u>pituitary gland</u>, muscle, and <u>brown fat</u> converts T<sub>4</sub> into the biologically active T<sub>3</sub>.

* Half of the T<sub>4</sub> is processed into biologically inactive T<sub>3</sub> (reverse T3).

* The <u>half-life</u> of T<sub>3</sub> is about one day (∼ 20 hours) and the <u>half-life</u> of T<sub>4</sub> is about one week (∼ 190 hours) .





| Detailed steps of <u>thyroid hormone synthesis</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steps | Description | Site |
| <br>1. Synthesis of <u>thyroglobulin</u> (TG) <br> | <br>1. * <u>Thyroglobulin</u> (TG) is produced in the <u>rough ER</u> of the follicular cells.<br>2. * TG is packed in <u>vesicles</u> in the <u>Golgi apparatus</u>.<br>3. * TG is released into the follicular lumen via exocytosis.<br><br> | <br>* <u>Thyrocyte</u> → follicular lumen<br><br> |
| <br>2. Uptake of iodide <br> | <br>1. * Basolateral transport<br>* Na<sup>+</sup>/I<sup>−</sup>-<u>symporter</u>: Uptake of iodide by <u>thyrocytes</u><br>2. * Apical transport<br>* Pendrin: <u>Iodine</u> diffuses to the apex of <u>the cell</u> and is transported into the follicular lumen via the <u>Pendrin transporter</u>.<br><br> | <br>* Blood vessel → <u>thyrocyte</u> → follicular lumen<br><br> |
| 3. Iodination of <u>thyroglobulin</u> | <br><br>* Thyroid peroxidase (<u>TPO</u>) <br>1. * Oxidation of iodide (I<sup>-</sup> → I<sub>2</sub>)<br>2. * Organification of the generated I<sub>2</sub> by covalently linking it with the <u>tyrosine</u> residues present in TG.<br>* Generates single (TG + <u>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub></u> + I<sub>2</sub>= monoiodotyrosine, MIT) or double-iodinated species of <u>tyrosine</u> (TG-MIT + <u>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub></u> + I<sub>2</sub>= diiodotyrosine, DIT)<br>3. * Coupling reaction: conjugation of iodinated <u>tyrosine</u> residues<br>1. * Two DIT molecules form <u>tetraiodothyronine</u>: DIT + DIT = T<sub>4</sub><br>2. * One MIT and one DIT form <u>triiodothyronine</u>: MIT + DIT = T<sub>3</sub><br><br>* <u>NADPH-oxidase</u>: apical enzyme that generates <u>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub></u> for <u>thyroid peroxidase</u><br>* Reaction: <u>NADPH</u> + H<sup>+</sup>+ O<sub>2</sub> → <u>NADP<sup>+</sup></u> + <u>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub></u><br><br><br> | <br>* In follicular lumen<br><br> |
| 4. Storage | <br>* Bound to <u>thyroglobulin</u><br><br> | <br>* In follicular lumen<br><br> |
| 5. Release | <br>1. * Reuptake of iodinated TG in <u>thyrocytes</u> via <u>endocytosis</u><br>2. * Fusion of <u>endocytosis</u> <u>vesicles</u> with <u>lysosome</u><br>3. * Proteolytic enzymes cleave TG to release T3, T4, DIT, and MIT<br>4. * T<sub>3</sub> (∼ 20%) and T<sub>4</sub> (∼ 80%) are released into the blood (via the MCT8 transporter)<br>5. * Deiodinase removes the <u>iodine</u> from the MIT and DIT, which is then redistributed to the intracellular I<sup>-</sup> pool (<u>iodine</u> salvage).<br><br> | <br>* <u>Thyrocyte</u> → <u>fenestrated capillary</u> network<br><br> |

#### Transport and degradation




<u>Thyroid hormones</u> are <u>lipophilic</u>, but due to their charged <u>amino acid derivatives</u>, they cannot simply diffuse across the <u>lipid bilayer</u>. Instead, they cross the plasma membrane with the help of transporter <u>proteins</u> (<u>facilitated diffusion</u>). Also, most of the circulating <u>thyroid hormones</u> are inactive and bound to transport <u>proteins</u>. Only a very small fraction (∼ 0.3%) is unbound and biologically active.




* Transport <u>proteins</u>

* Thyroxine-binding globulin (<u>TBG</u>)

* <u>TBG</u> binds most of the serum T<sub>3</sub>/T<sub>4.</sub>

* The bound fraction of T<sub>3</sub>/T<sub>4</sub> is biologically inactive.

* Hyperestrogenemia (e.g., <u>pregnancy</u>, <u>OCP</u> use) → ↑ <u>TBG</u> synthesis → ↓ free T<sub>3</sub>/T<sub>4</sub> in serum → ↑ <u>thyroid</u> <u>hormone</u> synthesis

* <u>Hypoproteinemia</u> (e.g., <u>nephrotic syndrome</u>, chronic <u>liver</u> disease) → ↓ <u>TBG</u> synthesis → ↑ free T<sub>3</sub>/T<sub>4</sub> in serum → ↓ <u>thyroid</u> <u>hormone</u> synthesis

* Transthyretin (<u>prealbumin</u>)

* Transport protein synthesized by the <u>liver</u> that carries <u>thyroxine</u> and the <u>retinol</u>-RBP complex

* <u>Negative acute phase protein</u>

* Decrease in <u>transthyretin</u> leads to the preservation of <u>amino acids</u> for <u>positive acute phase reactants</u>.

* Conditions that result in the accumulation of <u>transthyretin</u> include <u>senile cardiac amyloidosis</u>, <u>familial amyloid polyneuropathy</u>, and <u>familial amyloid cardiomyopathy</u>.

* <u>Albumin</u>

* Degradation (<u>liver</u>): after sulfation/<u>glucuronidation</u> (<u>biotransformation</u>), <u>thyroid hormones</u> are excreted via <u>bile</u>





#### Effect




In general, <u>thyroid hormones</u> increase the metabolic rate: oxygen and <u>energy consumption</u> as well as <u>thermogenesis</u> increase under their influence.




| Overview of <u>thyroid hormone</u> effects |  |
| --- | --- |
| Target organ | Effect |
| <u>Heart</u> | <br>* ↑ Expression of cardiac <u>β-receptors</u> (permissive effect on <u>catecholamines</u>)<br><br>* ↑ <u>Heart rate</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>Stroke volume</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>Cardiac output</u><br><br>* ↑ Contractility<br><br> |
| <u>Lungs</u> | <br><br>* Stimulation of the <u>respiratory center</u><br><br>* ↑ Respiratory rate<br><br>* Stimulation of <u>surfactant</u> production in <u>newborns</u><br><br>* ↑ Oxygenation due to increased <u>lung</u> <u>perfusion</u><br><br><br> |
| Nervous system | <br>* Maturation of the nervous system<br><br>* <u>Brain</u> maturation<br><br>* <u>Myelin</u> formation<br><br>* Axonal growth<br><br> |
| <u>Musculoskeletal system</u> | <br><br>* Increased development of <u>type II muscle fibers</u> (fast-twitch muscle fibers)<br><br>* Stimulation of bone growth via:<br><br>* Induction of <u>chondrocytes</u>, <u>osteoblasts</u>, and <u>osteoclasts</u>.<br><br>* Promotion of synthesis and secretion of <u>growth hormone</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Reproductive system [[2]](/library/tp0XrS) | <br><br>* <u>Fertility</u><br><br>* <u>Ovulation</u> and <u>menstruation</u><br><br><br> |
| Metabolism | <br><br>* ↑ <u>Basal metabolic rate</u> due to ↑ expression of <u>Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> ATPase</u> →↑ oxygen consumption, ↑ body temperature<br><br>* <u>Anabolism</u> of <u>proteins</u> (in high doses: <u>catabolism of proteins</u>)<br><br>* <u>Lipolysis</u> or liponeogenesis (depending on metabolic status)<br><br>* Stimulation of <u>carbohydrate</u> metabolism<br><br>* ↑ <u>Glucose</u> reabsorption<br><br>* ↑ <u>Gluconeogenesis</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>Glycogenolysis</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>Glucose</u> oxidation<br><br><br> |
| <u>Thermoregulation</u> | <br>* <u>Thermogenesis</u><br><br> |





#### Regulation




* <u>Hypothalamic-pituitary axis</u>   

* Stimulant (e.g., <u>stress</u>, extreme cold) → release of <u>thyrotropin-releasing hormone</u> (<u>TRH</u>) → ↑ secretion of <u>thyroid-stimulating hormone</u> (<u>TSH</u>) by the <u>pituitary</u> gland → ↑ synthesis and release of T<sub>3</sub> and T<sub>4</sub> by the <u>thyroid gland</u>

* Negative feedback by ↑ free T<sub>3</sub> or T<sub>4</sub>→ ↓ release of <u>TRH</u> and ↓ <u>pituitary</u> <u>sensitivity</u> to <u>TRH</u> → ↓ <u>thyroid</u> <u>hormones</u> synthesis

* <u>TSH</u> release can also be decreased by <u>somatostatin</u>, <u>dopamine</u>, and <u>glucocorticoids</u> (outside of the <u>hypothalamic</u>-<u>pituitary</u> axis).

* <u>TSH</u> stimulating <u>antibodies</u> in <u>Graves disease</u> result in the direct stimulation of the <u>pituitary gland</u> and <u>TSH</u> release. (See “<u>Graves disease</u>” for more information.)

* <u>TBG</u>: See “Transport and degradation” section above.

* <u>Wolff-Chaikoff effect</u>: a transient decrease in the production of <u>thyroid hormones</u> following the ingestion of a large amount of <u>iodine</u> via <u>thyroid peroxidase</u> inhibition

* Drugs

* Decreased T4 → T3 conversion: <u>glucocorticoids</u>, <u>propylthiouracil</u> (<u>PTU</u>), <u>β-blockers</u>

* Increased T4 → rT conversion: <u>growth hormone</u>, <u>glucocorticoids</u>

* <u>Thyroid peroxidase</u> inhibition: <u>PTU</u>, <u>methimazole</u>

> [!TIP]
> <u>TPO</u> is stimulated by <u>TSH</u> and inhibited by <u>PTU</u>, <u>methimazole</u>, and excess <u>iodine</u> (<u>Wolff-Chaikoff effect</u>), resulting in, respectively, high and low <u>thyroid hormone</u> levels.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Thyroid-stimulating hormone</u> (<u>TSH</u>) from the <u>pituitary gland</u> stimulates the basolateral uptake of <u>iodine</u> as well as the biosynthesis and release of <u>thyroid hormones</u>.




> [!TIP]
> <u>TSH</u> levels are very sensitive to <u>thyroid hormone</u> dysfunction. If <u>thyroid hormone</u> levels are very high, <u>TSH</u> can fall below detection limits and if they are very low, <u>TSH</u> increases markedly. Therefore, serum <u>TSH</u> is an important parameter for assessing <u>thyroid</u> function and is usually the first step in <u>thyroid</u> diagnostics.

## Embryology

### Overview




The <u>thyroid gland</u> develops in the <u>first trimester</u> of <u>pregnancy</u> from the fusion of the <u>median thyroid anlage</u> with the two <u>lateral thyroid anlages</u> derived from the <u>pharyngeal pouches</u>. Both follicular cells and <u>C cells</u> arise from pharyngeal <u>endoderm</u>  [[3]](/library/JPYsf6)[[4]](/library/6PYjf6)[[5]](/library/pPYLf6)




* Median thyroid anlage

* An <u>endodermal</u> thickening in the floor of the primordial <u>pharynx</u> between the 1<sup>st</sup> and 2<sup>nd</sup><u>pharyngeal pouches</u>

* This thickening becomes the <u>thyroid diverticulum</u>.

* Differentiates into the follicular cells of the <u>thyroid gland</u> (i.e., the major portion of the lobes and <u>isthmus</u> of the <u>thyroid gland</u>)

* Lateral thyroid anlagen (ultimobranchial bodies)

* Paired <u>endodermal</u> cell thickenings derived from the <u>4<sup>th</sup> branchial pouch</u>

* Fuse with the <u>median thyroid anlage</u>

* Differentiate into the <u>parafollicular C cells</u> of the <u>thyroid gland</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Follicular cells arise mainly from the <u>median thyroid anlage</u>.
> <u>Parafollicular C cells</u> arise mainly from the <u>lateral thyroid anlage</u>.




### Thyroid diverticulum




* A <u>thyroid gland</u> precursor that originates from the floor of the primordial <u>pharynx</u>

* It is located initially at the middle of the floor of the <u>pharynx</u>, near the base of the <u>tongue</u>, i.e., <u>foramen cecum</u> (<u>tongue</u>).

* It descends the neck, forming the thyroglossal duct, to settle into its adult <u>anatomical position</u>.

* The <u>thyroglossal duct</u> usually obliterates after the <u>thyroid gland</u> has descended.

* However, in about 50% of people, the <u>distal</u> portion of the duct remains as a clinically unremarkable pyramidal lobe of extra <u>thyroid</u> tissue

* <u>Thyroglossal cyst</u>: caused by a persistent <u>thyroglossal duct</u> (See “<u>Congenital neck masses</u>” for more details)

* Lingual thyroid: caused by failure in descent of the <u>thyroid gland</u> to its normal position during <u>embryogenesis</u>

* The <u>foramen cecum</u> of the <u>tongue</u> remains.

> During embryological <u>thyroid</u> migration, remnants of <u>thyroid</u> tissue can remain in the <u>tongue</u> (<u>lingual thyroid</u>) or elsewhere along the migration path. Incidental removal of <u>ectopic</u> <u>thyroid</u> tissue may result in <u>hypothyroidism</u> if the <u>ectopic</u> tissue is the only functioning <u>thyroid</u> tissue in the body.

## Parathyroid glands

### Overview




* Characteristics
* There are four, oval-shaped endocrine glands embedded in the <u>posterior</u> surface of the <u>thyroid gland</u>  

* Two superior <u>parathyroid glands</u>: located near the superior pole of the <u>thyroid gland</u> at the junction of cricoid and <u>thyroid</u> cartilages.

* Two inferior <u>parathyroid glands</u>: located in the area between the inferior poles of the <u>thyroid</u> lobes and the <u>superior mediastinum</u>.

* Function: secretion of <u>parathyroid hormone</u> (<u>PTH</u>) in response to low <u>calcium</u> serum levels

* Vasculature

* Arterial supply: <u>inferior thyroid arteries</u>

* Venous drainage: <u>thyroid</u> plexus of <u>veins</u>

* <u>Lymphatic drainage</u>: deep cervical nodes, paratracheal nodes

* Innervation: <u>thyroid</u> branches of the cervical <u>ganglia</u>





![Pharynx and parathyroid glands](media/uftgy19yhmoz2z4ka8guii7h.jpg)

Pharynx and parathyroid glands




### Microscopic anatomy



* Cell types

* <u>Adipocytes</u> (∼ 50%)

* Parathyroid cells (<u>parathyroid chief cells</u>) 

* Polygonal, <u>hormone</u>-secreting cells with round <u>nucleus</u>

* Produce and secrete <u>PTH</u>

* Have <u>calcium</u>-sensing <u>receptors</u> (<u>CaSR</u>), which detect changes in <u>calcium</u> concentration and modulate <u>PTH</u> secretion

* Oxyphil cells: red/pink <u>cytoplasm</u>; function not clear




![Parathyroid chief cells](media/scg2dsseapqmcad6a72ild71.jpg)

Parathyroid chief cells




### Function of <u>PTH</u>



* <u>PTH</u> increases serum <u>calcium</u> and decreases serum <u>phosphate</u> (see “<u>Calcium homeostasis</u>”). 

* High extracellular <u>calcium</u> → activation of <u>calcium</u>-sensitive <u>receptors</u> → ↓ <u>PTH</u> excretion

* Low extracellular <u>calcium</u> → inhibition of <u>calcium</u>-sensitive <u>receptors</u> → ↑ <u>PTH</u> excretion




![Regulation of calcium and phosphate metabolism](media/m1mufp2p8vmqt0ihbo0mz73r.jpg)

Regulation of calcium and phosphate metabolism




### <u>Embryology</u>




* Superior <u>parathyroid glands</u>: derived from the <u>fourth pharyngeal pouch</u>

* Inferior <u>parathyroid gland</u>: derived from the <u>third pharyngeal pouch</u>





> [!NOTE]
> <u>DiGeorge syndrome</u> is a <u>congenital T-cell immunodeficiency</u> that is caused by microdeletion at <u>chromosome</u> 22 (<u>22q11.2</u>). The deletion leads to defective development of the third and fourth <u>pharyngeal pouches</u>, resulting in aplastic parathyroids and <u>hypocalcemia</u> due to <u>PTH</u> deficiency.




### Clinical significance




* <u>Hyperparathyroidism</u>

* <u>Hypoparathyroidism</u>

* Pseudohypoparathyroidism

* <u>Thyroidectomy</u>

* <u>Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia</u>

* <u>Nelson syndrome</u>

* <u>MEN 1</u>

* <u>MEN 2A</u>

* <u>Osteitis fibrosa cystica</u>

* <u>Renal osteodystrophy</u>





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Surgery</u> of the <u>thyroid</u> and <u>parathyroid glands</u> can result in destroyed or removed <u>parathyroid glands</u> due to their variable position. This may result in <u>hypoparathyroidism</u> and <u>hypocalcemia</u>.
